name: Oxymatrine (a Sophora alkaloid)
short: 83 Sophora alkaloid poisonings: mostly minor; 1 needed cardiac monitoring (long QT, with ciprofloxacin). Hepatitis B trials: adverse reactions 7-8%, like placebo; a review: oral safety unproven.
text: Oxymatrine is an alkaloid found in Sophora flavescens (kushen) and related plants; it has been given as capsules or tablets by mouth and by injection into a vein or muscle. In a 24-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 216 people with chronic hepatitis B, adverse drug reactions occurred in 7.77% on oxymatrine capsules, 6.67% on oxymatrine injections and 8.82% on placebo (not significantly different). In a 52-week placebo-controlled trial in 144 people with chronic hepatitis B, adverse reactions occurred in 7.69% on oxymatrine and 6.15% on placebo (not significantly different), and in a 52-week placebo-controlled trial of capsules in 144 people with liver fibrosis from viral hepatitis, adverse event rates were similar in the two groups. However, a 2016 systematic review of 52 trials (5,227 participants) of oral oxymatrine for chronic hepatitis B rated the evidence as poor and concluded that its safety was still unproven. Liver injury: in mice given oxymatrine by mouth for 7 days, the highest dose tested (320 mg/kg) caused liver damage, and a 2025 poison-centre study says liver toxicity of Sophora alkaloids has been reported in laboratory and animal studies and isolated human case reports, although none was seen in its own 83 cases. Given by injection into a vein for psoriasis, oxymatrine was accompanied by only minor adverse effects in a 67-patient randomised trial, with significantly fewer adverse reactions than the comparison drug acitretin, and no adverse events were reported in 4 people with erythrodermic psoriasis. In 83 confirmed acute poisonings with Sophora alkaloids (including matrine and oxymatrine, mostly from Sophora flavescens taken by mouth, often in excessive doses) reported in Hong Kong, most effects were minor, mainly dizziness, vomiting and palpitations, and no acute liver or kidney injury was observed; one patient needed cardiac monitoring for a prolonged QT interval after also taking ciprofloxacin. No other interaction data were found in the cited sources.
